steps.prompt: Why do most AI products die on the data, not the algorithm?
steps.sub: Great models are everywhere now. The hard part is picking the RIGHT bet and proving the data can actually carry it. By the end you'll prioritize AI initiatives by value × feasibility, demand a non-ML baseline, spot data leakage before it burns you, and run a data-readiness check on a real product.

steps.prompt: The PM's four guardrails before any AI build.
steps.sub: Tap each card — these are the whole lesson in miniature.

cards.b: Plot every idea on business value vs technical/data feasibility. Ship high-value/high-feasibility first; time-box the high-value/low-feasibility ones as research spikes.
Always name the non-ML way (even 'predict the average'). If a simple rule already clears the bar, ML must beat it by enough to justify its cost.
Missing, dirty, biased, or not-legally-usable data kills more AI products than weak algorithms ever do.
If test data leaks into training, your metrics look amazing — then collapse in production. Trust the held-out number, never the training one.

steps.prompt: Three candidate AI bets. Where does each one go?
steps.sub: Tap an initiative, then a bin. Think value AND feasibility.

items.t: Predict which students will churn next month — we have 2 years of clean engagement + payment data
A tutor that grades free-text essays as reliably as a human examiner — we have almost no graded examples yet
Translate a lesson from English to Hindi inside the app
Auto-tag uploaded lesson PDFs by topic — we have thousands of labelled past lessons
Generic OCR to pull text out of scanned worksheets

hints: If the capability is a commodity (OCR, translation, generic LLM) and isn't your moat, lean API — don't build it.
High value but you can't yet prove it's doable on your data = a time-boxed spike, NOT a committed roadmap item.

steps.prompt: A high-value idea looks technically shaky right now. What's the right call?

options.t: Commit it to the roadmap with a hard ship date — high value means we must deliver it.
Run a time-boxed research spike to de-risk feasibility before committing anything.
Drop it forever — low feasibility means it's not worth touching.

steps.why: High-value/low-feasibility ideas are the classic trap: too valuable to ignore, too risky to promise. You buy information with a small, time-boxed spike — can the data support it? does a model beat baseline? — and only THEN decide to commit, kill, or re-scope. Promising a ship date before you've proven feasibility is how teams blow a quarter.
hints: Committing a ship date to something you can't yet prove is doable is how quarters get burned.
What's the cheapest way to BUY information about feasibility before betting the roadmap?

steps.prompt: Build it, buy it, or call an API? You need text translation inside your app.
steps.sub: Translation isn't your product's secret sauce.

options.t: Build your own translation model — owning everything is always safer.
Use a translation API — it's a commodity; build only where data/quality is your moat.
Skip the feature — translation is impossible to do well.

steps.why: Translation, generic OCR, and generic LLM chat are commodities — mature APIs do them better than you can cheaply build. Reserve your scarce build effort for the capability where YOUR proprietary data or quality bar is a genuine moat (e.g. tutoring on your own curriculum). Building a commodity from scratch spends moat-budget on something a customer can't tell apart.
hints: Is translation the thing customers choose YOU for, or table stakes anyone can buy?
Build where your data/quality is a moat; buy or API the commodities.

steps.prompt: Baselines & the data constraint — true or false?

statements.t: You should always define a non-ML baseline (even 'predict the average') before starting an ML project.
statements.why: Yes — the baseline is the bar. If a dumb rule already clears it, the ML project has to beat it by enough to justify its ongoing cost.

statements.t: If a simple rule already meets the business bar, the ML version only needs to roughly tie it to be worth building.
statements.why: No — ML carries real ongoing cost (data pipelines, monitoring, drift, on-call). It must beat the baseline by ENOUGH to justify that, not just tie.

statements.t: Most AI products fail because the team didn't have a clever enough algorithm.
statements.why: No — they mostly fail on DATA: missing, dirty, biased, or not legally usable. 'We have a great algorithm' is almost never the real bottleneck.

statements.t: Data that the team has no legal right or consent to use for this purpose is effectively unusable, no matter how good it is.
statements.why: Right — rights and consent are a hard gate. Great data you can't legally use for THIS purpose is, for the project, no data at all.

hints: A baseline is the bar to beat; remember ML has ongoing cost, not just one-time cost.
Where do most AI products actually break — the model, or the data feeding it?

steps.prompt: Train / validation / test — and the leak that fakes success.
steps.sub: Tap each card. This split is your honesty mechanism.

cards.b: The data the model studies to fit its parameters. The model is allowed to 'see' this.
A separate slice for picking settings (which model, which knobs). Used to tune — never the final verdict.
A held-out slice the model never touched. This is your best guess at real-world performance — guard it.
If test (or future) info sneaks into training, scores look brilliant in the lab, then crater in production. Trust the clean test number.

steps.prompt: Your model scores 99% in testing but flops in production. The engineer admits the test rows were also used during training. What happened?
steps.sub: This is the single most common metric trap in AI products.

options.t: The production users are just unusual — the 99% is the real number.
Data leakage — test data leaked into training, inflating the score. The honest number is much lower.
The model is overconfident; lowering the threshold will fix the gap.

steps.why: Classic data leakage. When test rows are seen during training, the model effectively memorizes the answers, so the 'test' score measures recall, not generalization. It looks like 99% in the lab and collapses on truly unseen production data. The fix is a clean held-out test set the model never touches — and as PM, you trust THAT number, never the inflated training one.
hints: If the model already saw the test rows while learning, what is the test score really measuring?
A score that's great in the lab but bad in production is the signature of leakage, not unusual users.

steps.prompt: Data-readiness check: tap EVERY question a PM must answer before greenlighting an ML build.
steps.sub: Pick all that belong on the gate.
chips: Is the data representative of real production inputs?
Is it labelled well — and who keeps labelling it going forward?
Do we have the rights/consent to use it for THIS purpose?
Does it stay fresh via a pipeline, not a one-off dump?
What biases or gaps exist — and who could get hurt?
What's the non-ML baseline we must beat?
Is the algorithm the trendiest one on social media this week?
steps.why: The first six are the data-readiness gate: representative, labelled (with an ongoing labelling plan), legally usable, kept fresh by a pipeline, audited for bias/harm, and measured against a baseline. The last one — chasing the trendiest algorithm — is exactly the distraction this lesson warns against. Data readiness, not algorithm fashion, decides whether the product survives.
hints: Everything about the DATA and the BASELINE belongs on the gate.
One chip is about algorithm hype, not readiness — leave it out.

steps.prompt: TrigunAI gut-check: would each idea pass the data-readiness gate today?
steps.sub: Tap an idea, then a bin — judge the DATA, not the dream.
buckets: ⚠️ Blocked on data (not on the algorithm)

items.t: Summarize each published lesson — we have thousands of clean lesson texts and a generic LLM to call
Predict student churn — but we've only run for 3 weeks, so almost no one has actually churned yet
Auto-grade essays like a human examiner — we have only a handful of hand-graded examples and no labelling plan
Recommend the next lesson — we have months of representative click + completion data

hints: No labels, no history, or unrepresentative data = blocked on data, however good the model is.
Plenty of clean, representative, rights-clear data + a clear baseline = likely passes.

steps.sub: Not graded. Run the gate on something you actually want to build.

fields.label: Name one AI feature you'd love to ship. What data would it stand on?
fields.ph: e.g. predict churn — needs 12+ months of engagement + payment history

fields.label: Which data-readiness question is your biggest risk — and what's the non-ML baseline?
fields.ph: e.g. risk = no labels yet; baseline = flag anyone inactive 14+ days

statements.t: High-value but low-feasibility ideas should be time-boxed research spikes, not committed roadmap items.
statements.why: Right — you de-risk with a small spike before committing, instead of promising a ship date you can't yet back.

statements.t: For a commodity capability that isn't your moat, prefer an API over building from scratch.
statements.why: Yes — save build effort for where your data/quality is a real moat; buy the commodities.

statements.t: A held-out test set the model never saw gives a more honest estimate than the training score.
statements.why: Correct — that's the whole point of the split. Trust the clean test number; the training number is biased upward.

statements.t: Once you've collected data once, you're set — AI products don't need an ongoing data pipeline.
statements.why: No — a one-off dump goes stale. Real products need data kept fresh by a pipeline, plus ongoing labelling and bias monitoring.

hints: Three of these you just practised; one describes the 'one-off dump' anti-pattern.
Which statement ignores that data and the world keep changing?
